content:
Lupus (systemic lupus erythematosus, or SLE) is an autoimmune condition that commonly causes joint pain and stiffness, often in the hands, wrists and knees. Unlike rheumatoid arthritis, lupus joint pain rarely causes lasting joint damage. Lupus can also affect the skin, kidneys, blood and other organs, so it needs specialist care. Treatment can control it well for most people.

Joint symptoms in lupus

Most people with lupus have joint symptoms at some point:

  • pain and stiffness, often in the small joints of hands and wrists, and in knees
  • symptoms on both sides of the body
  • swelling, sometimes mild
  • morning stiffness
  • pain that moves between joints and comes and goes with flares

Joint deformity is uncommon, although some people develop a reversible drift of the fingers called Jaccoud's arthropathy.

How it differs from rheumatoid arthritis

RA and lupus can look similar at first. Differences include:

  • RA is more likely to cause permanent joint damage
  • lupus often comes with other symptoms such as rashes, mouth ulcers and kidney problems
  • blood tests differ: lupus is linked with ANA and anti-dsDNA antibodies, RA with rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP

Some people have overlap features of both.

Other symptoms of lupus

  • extreme tiredness
  • rashes, especially a butterfly-shaped rash across the cheeks and nose, often triggered by sunlight
  • mouth or nose ulcers
  • hair loss
  • fevers
  • fingers that turn white or blue in the cold (Raynaud's)
  • chest pain when breathing in
  • swollen ankles or frothy urine, which can be signs of kidney involvement
  • dry eyes and mouth
  • low mood, anxiety and memory problems

Who gets lupus

Lupus is much more common in women, usually starting between 15 and 45. It is more common in people of African, Caribbean, Asian and Chinese heritage.

Diagnosis

Diagnosis can take time because symptoms vary and come and go. Your GP may arrange blood tests including ANA. A positive ANA alone does not mean you have lupus, as it is found in many healthy people. If lupus is suspected, you will be referred to a rheumatologist. Urine tests check the kidneys.

Treatment

  • hydroxychloroquine is the main long-term treatment for most people. It helps joints, skin and fatigue and reduces flares. Regular eye checks are needed.
  • NSAIDs may ease joint pain if suitable for you.
  • steroids in the lowest effective dose for flares
  • other immune-suppressing medicines, such as methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate, for more active disease
  • biologics, such as belimumab, for some people

Self-care

  • protect your skin from the sun with high-factor sunscreen and covering up
  • pace yourself and plan rest
  • stay active with gentle exercise to help joints and fatigue
  • do not smoke, as it can make lupus worse and reduce how well hydroxychloroquine works
  • look after your heart, as lupus increases cardiovascular risk
  • plan pregnancy with your team, as some medicines need changing and pregnancy needs close monitoring

Living with lupus

Lupus is unpredictable, but many people live full lives with treatment. Keep regular appointments and blood and urine tests, and report new symptoms early.

Questions to ask your rheumatologist

  • Which parts of my body is lupus affecting?
  • How will we monitor my kidneys and blood?
  • How often do I need eye checks on hydroxychloroquine?
  • What should I do in a flare, and who do I contact?
  • Is it safe for me to plan a pregnancy, and when?

Keeping a symptom diary, including photos of rashes or swollen joints, can help your team see patterns between appointments. Support groups for people with lupus can also offer practical tips and reassurance, especially soon after diagnosis.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • chest pain or sudden breathlessness, a seizure, sudden confusion, or severe headache
  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
